items.prompt: Look at the white rook. What is the name of the square it stands on?

claims.statement: A white rook stands on h1 and can move to exactly these squares.

hints: Files are the letters, a to h from left to right as White sees the board. Which file is the rook on?
Ranks are the numbers, 1 at White's side. Which rank is the rook on?
The rook is on the last file and the first rank: letter first, then number.
items.explain: The rook is in the corner on the far right of White's side: file h, rank 1, so the square is h1.

items.prompt: Move the white pawn to the square d4.

claims.statement: The pawn on d2 can go to d4.

hints: Find the d file first: it is the fourth letter, a-b-c-d.
Then find rank 4: count up four rows from White's side.
The pawn on d2 can jump two squares on its first move.
items.explain: d is the fourth file and 4 is the fourth rank. The pawn on d2 moves two squares forward to d4.

feedback_by_move.d2d3: d3 is one square forward. The target square was d4.

items.prompt: Play the move Nf3. (N stands for knight.)

claims.statement: The knight on g1 can go to f3.
The other knight cannot reach f3.

hints: N is the letter for the knight. Which white pieces are knights?
The move ends on f3. Find file f and rank 3.
The knight on g1 jumps to f3.
items.explain: Nf3 means the knight goes to f3. White has two knights, but only the one on g1 can reach f3 from here.

items.prompt: Play the move Bc4. (B stands for bishop.)

claims.statement: The bishop on f1 can go to c4.

hints: B is the letter for the bishop. White's bishop on f1 is the one that can move.
Find the square c4: third file, fourth rank.
The bishop slides from f1 along the diagonal to c4.
items.explain: Bc4 means the bishop goes to c4. The bishop on f1 slides along the diagonal f1-e2-d3-c4.

items.prompt: What is the name of the square the white rook stands on?

claims.statement: A white rook stands on a1 and can move to exactly these squares.

hints: The file is a letter. The rank is a number.
This board is shown from White's side, with rank 1 at the bottom.
The rook is on the left-hand corner at White's side.
items.explain: The rook is on file a and rank 1, so the square is a1.

items.prompt: The same position, but the board is turned around so you see it from Black's side. What is the name of the square the white rook stands on?

claims.statement: The same white rook still stands on a1.

hints: Do not go by where the rook looks like it is. Square names belong to the board.
The rook has not moved. Only your view of the board changed.
Ranks still count from White's side, so the rook is on rank 1 whichever way you look.
items.explain: Turning the board around changes how it looks, not the names. The rook has not moved, so it is still on a1, which now appears in the top-right corner.

items.prompt: Play the move Nxe5. (The x means a capture.)

claims.statement: The knight on f3 can capture on e5.
Exactly one white piece attacks e5.

hints: Which letter is the knight, and where is White's knight now?
x means capture, so there is a black piece on e5.
The knight on f3 jumps to e5 and removes the black pawn.
items.explain: Nxe5 means the knight captures on e5. The knight on f3 is the only white piece that can reach that square.

items.prompt: Black to move. What is the name of the square the black queen stands on?

claims.statement: A black queen stands on d8 and can move to exactly these squares.

hints: Black's pieces start on rank 8 and rank 7.
The black queen starts right next to the black king, on the same rank.
The queen is on the fourth file, d, on the eighth rank.
items.explain: The black queen has not moved from her starting square: file d, rank 8, so d8.

items.prompt: What is the name of the square the white knight stands on?

claims.statement: A white knight stands on c6 and can move to exactly these squares.

hints: Find the file first: count the columns from the left, a-b-c.
Then count the rows up from White's side.
Third file, sixth rank.
items.explain: The knight is on the third file (c) and the sixth rank, so it stands on c6.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white rook can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the rook on d4 can move to.

hints: A rook moves in straight lines: along its rank and along its file.
Go one direction at a time and stop when you meet a piece.
You may land on an enemy piece (that is a capture) but never on your own, and you cannot jump past anything.
items.explain: The rook can reach 11 squares. It can capture the black pawn on d7, and its line ends there. It stops before its own pawn on b4.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white bishop can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the bishop on d4 can move to.

hints: A bishop moves only along diagonals, in four directions.
Go one diagonal at a time and stop when you meet a piece.
Your own pawn on b2 stops one direction early, and the black pawn on f6 can be captured but not passed.
items.explain: The bishop can reach 9 squares. It can capture the black pawn on f6, and its line ends there. It stops before its own pawn on b2.

items.prompt: Can the white rook go to d8 in one move? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The rook can slide from d4 to d8: d5, d6 and d7 are empty.

hints: Look at every square between the rook and d8.
A rook needs a clear line to slide along.
items.explain: The squares d5, d6 and d7 are empty, so the rook slides straight to d8.

items.prompt: Now a black pawn stands on d6. Can the white rook go to d8 in one move? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The rook cannot get from d4 to d8.
It can capture the pawn on d6.

hints: Look at every square between the rook and d8.
Can a rook jump over a piece?
items.explain: The pawn on d6 is in the way. A rook cannot jump, so it can capture the pawn on d6 but cannot reach d8.

items.prompt: A black pawn stands on f6. Can the white bishop go to f6? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The bishop can capture on f6.

hints: Is f6 on one of the bishop's diagonals?
Whose piece stands on f6?
items.explain: f6 is on the bishop's diagonal and holds an enemy pawn, so the bishop can capture it.

items.prompt: Now the pawn on f6 is White's own pawn. Can the white bishop go to f6? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The bishop cannot land on f6.
It can still go to e5, just before the pawn.

hints: Is f6 on one of the bishop's diagonals?
Whose piece stands on f6 now?
items.explain: A piece may never land on a square holding its own side's piece. The bishop can reach e5 but not f6.

items.prompt: The rook can capture one of the black pawns on its lines. Capture one.

claims.statement: The rook can capture the pawn on g3.
The rook can capture the pawn on d7.
The rook cannot reach a3: its own knight is in the way.

hints: Look at each black pawn. Is it on the rook's rank or file?
Is anything standing in between the rook and the pawn?
Check the pawn on a3: what stands on b3?
items.explain: The rook can take the pawn on g3 or on d7 along open lines. It cannot take a3, because its own knight on b3 blocks the way.

items.prompt: The bishop can capture one of the black pawns. Which move does it?

claims.statement: The bishop can capture on f4.
It cannot capture on g4.
These are all the squares the bishop can go to.

hints: A bishop only moves on diagonals. Which pawn stands on a diagonal of c1?
From c1 the long diagonal goes d2, e3, f4, g5, h6.
f4 is on that diagonal and nothing stands between.
items.explain: f4 is on the bishop's diagonal c1-d2-e3-f4. The pawn on g4 is on no diagonal of c1. A bishop stays on one colour of square for the whole game, and c1 and g4 are different colours.

items.prompt: Which of White's pieces can move to e5 (capturing the black pawn)? Rook, bishop, both, or neither?

claims.statement: The rook can move to e5.
The bishop can move to e5.

hints: For each piece, look along its lines toward e5.
Check for anything standing between the piece and e5.
The rook comes up the e-file; the bishop comes along a diagonal.
items.explain: The rook slides up the open e-file and the bishop uses the open diagonal b2-c3-d4-e5. Both can capture on e5.

items.prompt: Which of White's pieces can capture the black knight on c6? Rook, bishop, both, or neither?

claims.statement: The rook can move to c6.
The bishop cannot move to c6.

hints: For each piece, trace its line toward c6.
The bishop on g2 looks aimed at c6. Is the diagonal clear?
Look at d5.
items.explain: The rook comes up the open c-file. The bishop's diagonal g2-f3-e4-d5-c6 is blocked by the black pawn on d5, so only the rook can capture on c6.

items.prompt: Which of White's pieces can move to b6? Rook, bishop, both, or neither?

claims.statement: The rook cannot move to b6.
The bishop can move to b6.

hints: Trace each piece's lines. Does either line pass through b6?
The rook on a1 uses the a-file and the first rank.
The bishop uses diagonals through d4.
items.explain: The bishop reaches b6 along the diagonal d4-c5-b6. The rook on a1 only travels along the a-file and the first rank, which do not include b6.

items.prompt: Which of White's pieces can capture the black pawn on h7? Rook, bishop, both, or neither?

claims.statement: The rook cannot move to h7.
The bishop cannot move to h7.

hints: Trace each piece's lines toward h7.
Rooks use ranks and files, bishops use diagonals.
Count the diagonals that pass through f1, and the lines through d1.
items.explain: The rook on d1 uses the d-file and the first rank. The bishop on f1 uses the diagonals f1-a6 and f1-h3. None of those lines includes h7.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white queen can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on d4 can move to.

hints: The queen moves like a rook and a bishop together: straight lines and diagonals.
Go in all eight directions, one at a time, and stop at the first piece.
Two white pawns shorten two of the lines. Two black pawns can be captured, and the lines stop there.
items.explain: The queen can reach 18 squares. It can capture the black pawn on f6 and the black pawn on c5, and each of those lines ends there. It stops before its own pawn on b4, pawn on d2 and king on g1.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white king can move to. Watch out for the black rook.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king on e4 can move to.
The black rook attacks e5.
Nothing black attacks d4.

hints: The king moves one square in any direction.
But a king may never move onto a square the enemy attacks. Which squares does the rook attack?
The rook attacks the whole fifth rank, so d5, e5 and f5 are forbidden.
items.explain: The king has eight neighbouring squares, but the black rook covers the whole fifth rank, so d5, e5 and f5 are off limits. Five squares remain.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white king can move to.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the king on e4 can move to.
The black king attacks e5.
The black king attacks f5.

hints: A king may not move onto a square the enemy attacks. Does the black king attack anything?
Kings attack all the squares next to them. Which of white's neighbouring squares are next to the black king?
e5 and f5 touch the king on f6. Kings can never stand next to each other.
items.explain: The black king on f6 touches e5 and f5, so the white king cannot step there. Two kings can never stand on neighbouring squares. Six squares remain.

items.prompt: Can the white king capture the black knight on d5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The king can capture on d5.
No black piece guards d5.

hints: The king can capture an enemy piece on a neighbouring square. Is the knight on a neighbouring square?
But the king may not move onto an attacked square. Does any black piece attack d5?
items.explain: No black piece attacks d5, so the king may take the knight.

items.prompt: A black pawn now stands on c6. Can the white king capture the black knight on d5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The king cannot capture on d5.
The pawn on c6 guards d5.

hints: Is the knight on a neighbouring square? Yes, so look at what else changed.
Which black piece attacks d5 now?
Pawns attack the squares diagonally in front of them. The pawn on c6 attacks d5.
items.explain: The black pawn on c6 guards d5. If the king took the knight it would land on an attacked square, and that is never allowed.

items.prompt: Tap every white piece that can capture the black bishop on g4.

claims.statement: The rook can capture on g4.
The queen can capture on g4.
The knight can capture on g4.
Exactly three white pieces attack g4.

hints: Check each white piece in turn: rook, queen, knight, king, pawns.
Rooks use straight lines, queens use both, and knights jump in an L shape.
Three pieces can capture: the rook along the fourth rank, the queen on a diagonal, and one jump.
items.explain: The rook slides along the fourth rank, the queen uses the diagonal d1-e2-f3-g4, and the knight jumps from e3 to g4. The king and the pawns cannot reach g4.

items.prompt: Can the white knight on c4 move to b6 in one move? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The knight can jump from c4 to b6.

hints: A knight jumps in an L: two squares one way, then one square sideways.
From c4: go up two squares, then one to the left.
items.explain: From c4, two squares up is c6 and one to the left is b6. That is an L-shaped jump, so the answer is yes.

items.prompt: Tap the white piece that can capture the black pawn on f7. (It is not a good idea, but can anyone do it?)

claims.statement: The bishop on c4 can capture on f7.
Exactly one white piece attacks f7.

hints: Check each white piece. Which one has a line toward f7?
Look at the diagonals.
The bishop's diagonal c4-d5-e6-f7 is open.
items.explain: Only the bishop on c4 reaches f7, along the open diagonal c4-d5-e6-f7. Being able to capture is not the same as it being a good idea.

items.prompt: Can any white piece capture the black rook on a8 right now? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: No white piece attacks a8.
The white rook cannot capture on a8.

hints: Check the white rook, the bishop, the knight, and so on, one at a time.
The bishop on b2 is on a diagonal. Where does it go?
The white rook on e1 uses the e-file and the first rank.
items.explain: No white piece has a line to a8: the rook on e1 uses the e-file and the first rank, the bishop on b2 is not on a diagonal that reaches a8, and the knight on c3 jumps elsewhere.
